summary: Door County light on the northwest tip of Washington Island, first shown in 1933; the Coast Guard owns it and its grounds and tower are closed.

structures.note: The first tower of the 1933 light, per LighthouseFriends. Rowlett says the present tower replaced a square pyramidal skeletal tower; the date of the change is not given.
80 ft (24 m) per Rowlett; LighthouseFriends gives 67 ft. Focal plane 220 ft (67 m) per Rowlett and LighthouseFriends.

access.note: Coast Guard grounds and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). Washington Island is reached by car ferry from Northport.

events.note: Flashing white light of 280 candlepower established September 5, 1933, on a white skeleton pyramidal tower; focal plane 215 ft; visible eleven miles (LighthouseFriends). Rowlett gives the station as established 1933.
White skeleton pyramidal tower erected for the 1933 light.

notes_for_editor: (1) Thin station: two web sources (LighthouseFriends; Rowlett's directory) agree on the 1933 establishment; the USLHS light list (2004 only) adds the characteristic and 'On skeleton tower'. No primary source was read for the 1933 establishment. (2) No roster: roster.py finds no USLHS place for Boyer Bluff (the nearest name is Eagle Bluff, a different Door County light). No keeper is named in any source read, so the story has no keepers section. The story does not say that no keepers existed. (3) The corpus Lighthouse Service Bulletins for 1933 and 1934 have no mention of Boyer Bluff in OCR (loose-pattern searches for Boyer, Bluff, Washington Island, Porte des Morts, Pilot Island). The September or October 1933 issue might carry the establishment; not found. (4) Tower height disagreement: LighthouseFriends 67 ft; Rowlett 80 ft (24 m); the USLHS 2004 entry prints the numbers 80 and 220 without labels, which agree with Rowlett. (5) Range: LighthouseFriends gives 'visible for eleven miles' for the 1933 light, with no unit; the record's range_nm 6.1 (nominal, from ENC) is not reconciled with it. (6) Access: the record sets visit.boat_only true, but LighthouseFriends says Washington Island is reached by car ferry from Northport, so the island is reachable by road once there. The Boyer Bluff site's road access is not stated in any source read. Human review suggested. (7) Replacement of the 1933 tower by the present tower: no date in any source read (Rowlett: 'date unknown' for the station record; the tower replacement is not dated). (8) Same-name trap: the Evening Star (Washington, D.C.), February 19, 1933, page 9, mentions 'Boyer's Bluff' in a description of a Lake Michigan channel boundary near Bark River, Michigan. That is a different place and is not used. (9) Newspapers: Chronicling America 'Boyer Bluff' 1930-1945 returned five pages (Florida, Connecticut, Arizona and Washington titles); none concerns this light. (10) The Wisconsin Harbor Towns page (wisconsinharbortowns.net) and BloomWX give conflicting heights and a 1953 build date; BloomWX is not reliable on this and is not cited; the Harbor Towns page did not render. (11) Washington Island's own history site carries an excerpt from Karges' Keepers of the Lights about Rock Island; it has no Boyer Bluff material and is not cited. (12) Corpus status: the Bulletin text for 1933 is present in the corpus; grep finds no Boyer Bluff entry. (13) Fact-check 2026-10-28: every evidence quote was found in its cached source. The story now dates the 2012 flash and 67-ft tower to LighthouseFriends' 2012 description rather than stating them in the present tense; the tower is given as triangular cylindrical per Rowlett; the USLHS entry is described as a reproduction of the 2004 Coast Guard Light List; Rowlett's passage remarks are framed as the directory's description of the waters, not this light's history; focal plane and tower heights carry metres. LighthouseFriends gives 'eleven miles' without a unit, so the story does not call it nautical. (14) The corpus grep for 'Boyer Bluff' in the 1933-34 Bulletins returned no hits, but the tool reported that it searched 0 of 3 volumes, so that negative is weak; a human could check the September-October 1933 Bulletin directly.
